blocks.prompt: The Bird With a Radiator on His Head
blocks.text: A rooster is a male chicken. The red bumpy crown on his head is called a comb. The two red flaps under his beak are called wattles. Chickens do not sweat. Blood moves through the comb and the wattles, and the warm blood cools down there. So the comb is a bit like a radiator on his head. A rooster crows to say this place is mine. He crows at dawn. He also crows all day long. If a hawk flies over, the rooster makes a different sound. It is a warning. The hens run for cover.

blocks.prompt: The Clock Inside the Rooster
blocks.text: Everyone knows the rooster crows at dawn. Here is the strange part. He starts before the sun comes up. For a long time people thought the rooster was just waking up to the first light. Scientists in Japan decided to test it. They kept roosters in a room with dim light that never changed. There was no sunrise in that room at all. The roosters crowed anyway. Every day, right around the time dawn would have happened, they lifted their heads and crowed. That means the rooster is not answering the sun. He is carrying a clock inside his body. The clock runs on its own, close to twenty four hours, and it tells him dawn is coming before dawn arrives. Sunlight still helps. It nudges the clock and keeps it set to the real day, the way you nudge a watch that runs a little fast. But take the sun away and the rooster keeps time anyway.

blocks.prompt: The Rooster Who Goes First
blocks.text: Put a group of chickens together and within a few days they will have sorted themselves out. One bird can peck any other bird. The next bird can peck everyone except the first. All the way down the line there is a bird at the bottom who can peck nobody. Nothing about this is a metaphor. When people say pecking order, they are talking about actual chickens doing actual pecking. A young Norwegian named Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe noticed this in his family's flock when he was about ten years old. He kept notebooks. He gave the hens names and recorded who pecked whom. Years later he turned those notebooks into the first scientific study of a social ladder in animals, and the phrase he coined escaped the henhouse and never came back. Roosters live on that ladder too, and it shows up in their voices. Researchers watching a flock at dawn found that the top rooster crows first. Every morning. The second rooster waits for him and crows next, then the third, all the way down. If the top rooster is removed, the second one starts crowing first within days. The order in the sound is the order in the flock. Rank buys other things as well. A high ranking rooster does something called tidbitting: he finds a bit of food, makes a fast clucking call, then picks the food up and drops it again and again until a hen comes over to take it. He rarely eats it himself. A low ranking rooster who tries this often gets chased off before a hen arrives.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A crow measures over 100 decibels at his own ear
Opening his beak shuts his ear canal

Every chicken descends from the red junglefowl

blocks.prompt: A Voice Built for Trouble
blocks.text: A rooster's crow is not a song. It is closer to an announcement, and it is startlingly loud. When researchers in Belgium placed tiny microphones beside a rooster's ears and let him crow, the readings came back above a hundred decibels, louder than a lawn mower running next to your head. A sound like that, delivered at point blank range, should damage the ear that produces it. It does not, and the reason is a small piece of engineering. When a rooster crows he opens his beak all the way. That movement drags soft tissue across the ear canal, closing it like a shutter, and a bony part of the skull shifts over the eardrum at the same moment. The rooster deafens himself for the exact length of his own noise, then opens back up. He never hears his loudest sound at full volume. The rooster's other calls are quieter and much stranger. He does not have one alarm. He has at least two, and they mean different things. A hawk overhead gets a thin, drawn out shriek. A fox or a snake on the ground gets a fast, sharp cackle. Hens respond correctly to each one even when no predator is in sight. Play a recording of the aerial call and the flock crouches and looks up. Play the ground call and they stand tall and scan sideways. The sound is not just noise pushed out by fear. It carries information about what kind of danger is coming. Here is the detail that unsettles biologists. A rooster alone in a pen, watching a fake hawk glide overhead, often says nothing at all. Put a hen in the pen with him and he calls. The danger has not changed. His audience has. Researchers call this the audience effect, and it means the rooster is not simply reacting. Some part of him is registering who is listening. That is a lot of machinery for a farm bird. It helps to remember what he actually is. Every chicken alive descends from the red junglefowl, a wary forest bird from Southeast Asia that spent its life dodging things that hunt from above and things that hunt from below. The rooster in the yard is running instructions written for a jungle.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Bird That Knows When Dawn Is Coming

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Gallus gallus domesticus, descended from the red junglefowl
Free running crow rhythm of about 23.8 hours
Beak opening seals the ear canal during the crow
Dominant rooster crows first, others follow by rank
Pecking order named by Schjelderup-Ebbe in the 1920s
Domesticated roughly 3,500 years ago in Southeast Asia

blocks.prompt: The Bird That Predicts the Sunrise
blocks.text: Long before there were alarm clocks, there was a bird that made a noise at dawn, and people organized their mornings around it. The assumption underneath that arrangement seems obvious. Light arrives, the bird notices, the bird crows. The obvious version turns out to be wrong. In 2013 a research team at Nagoya University in Japan tested it properly. They kept roosters in rooms lit by a dim glow that never brightened and never faded, with no sunrise to react to and nothing visible changing at all. The roosters crowed anyway, and they did not crow randomly. Each bird produced a burst of crowing on a cycle of roughly twenty three and eight tenths hours, close to a day but not exactly a day. That slight drift is the signature of an internal clock running under its own power. The rooster is not reporting the sunrise. He is predicting it. Daylight, when it is available, does not create the rhythm. It corrects it, nudging a clock that would otherwise wander a few minutes out of step with the sky. The crowing itself is a feat of a different order. Microphones placed beside a rooster's own ears record his crow at over a hundred decibels, a level that would ruin human hearing with repeated exposure. Anatomists at the University of Antwerp went looking for the protection and found it. Opening the beak fully, which a rooster must do to crow, drags soft tissue across the ear canal and shifts a bony plate over the eardrum. The bird seals his own ears in the instant he shouts, and the shutter opens again when the beak closes. No decision is involved. The mechanism is wired to the jaw. What the crow means is less obvious than it sounds. It is not a greeting and it is not joy. It is a territorial claim, roughly translatable as this ground is occupied and I am the one occupying it. In a flock the claim is made in strict sequence. The dominant rooster crows first each morning and the others follow in descending rank, waiting their turn. Remove the dominant bird and the second in line begins crowing first within a matter of days. The pecking order, a phrase a Norwegian schoolboy named Thorleif Schjelderup-Ebbe coined in the 1920s after years of notebooks on his family's hens, is audible before it is visible. None of this equipment was built for the farmyard. Every chicken on Earth descends from the red junglefowl, a nervous, sharp eyed bird of Southeast Asian forests, domesticated roughly three and a half thousand years ago. A forest is a place where dawn matters, where announcing your territory across dense cover is safer than showing yourself, and where death arrives from the air and from the ground in different shapes requiring different warnings. The rooster still gives separate alarm calls for the two, and he still calls more readily when a hen is there to hear it than when he is standing alone. We have kept the bird for meat and eggs and, for a long stretch of history, for the noise. Roosters sit on church steeples across Europe and on barn roofs across America, hammered flat into weathervanes, pointing at the wind. It is a strange honor for a chicken. It is also, if you think about what the animal actually does at dawn, a fairly accurate one. We put the bird that keeps time on the highest point we have.
